Pele Yoetz 380:11: It might seem that eating bread alone is better than fasting, since eating fulfills the positive Torah commandment of Birkat HaMazon plus several rabbinic commandments, while fasting fulfills no such commandment at all - yet since holy men fasted days and nights, the secret of fasting must be great and bear more fruit above than commandments fulfilled through eating. But for one who is weak of strength, or who is engaged in Heaven's work, or who has the capacity to afflict his soul without becoming weakened (as above), or who can bear lighter forms of suffering by his own good will (wearing sackcloth, lashes, enduring flea or mosquito bites, and the like) - all this counts greatly toward restraining transgression and removing sin, and such a person has no excuse to say he lacked the strength, since these things involve no real weakening. Likewise, being among those who are insulted yet do not insult back, rejoicing in suffering, forgoing one's own honor, and similar things that serve as segulot for atonement (as written above under the entry Segulah) - people are "cut off at the legs" when they fail to fast and say they lack the strength: what will they answer on the day of reckoning for not having done even these things?
Pele Yoetz 380:12: Since fasting is analogous to a sacrifice, repentance must be joined with it just as it was needed with a sacrifice - without repentance, it is said of it (Proverbs 21:27), "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination." It is possible that fasting without any element of repentance still earns good reward for the effort and bears fruit above and effects atonement through God's kindnesses, since He has not despised or loathed the affliction of the afflicted; but the essence of fasting is that one's uncircumcised heart be subdued, that he examine his deeds and loosen the cords of wickedness, abandon his wicked way, make fences and restrictions for himself, and return to the Lord who will have mercy on him. Regarding communal fasts specifically, Maimonides already wrote (Laws of Fasts, ch. 5, 1) that fasting over troubles that have already passed gives or adds nothing - what was, was; rather the essence of the fast is that we take to heart that the troubles came because of our ancestors' sins, and we have still not been purified, and our deeds are like theirs, and therefore we have not been saved, and so we shall return to the Name and He will have mercy on us.
Pele Yoetz 380:13: One must be careful on the fast day against every stumbling block and sinful thought, not being like one who immerses [in a mikveh] while holding an impure creeping thing, or like one who plants trees while cutting down plantings on the other side. Above all one must guard against anger, since on a fast day one is especially prone to anger over anything at all - and since one who becomes angry is like an idolater, the loss is greater than the gain, and it would be better not to fast at all than to fast only to end up in strife and quarrel; therefore let him gather great strength and stand guard so as not to labor in vain. Also among the conditions of the fast is that he give to charity the measure of what he would have eaten, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 6b), "The reward of the fast is charity." And they further said (Sanhedrin 35a) that any fast where charity is not given before nightfall is as though blood were shed. And they hinted that the word "ta'anit" (fast) is a notarikon for "tet ani" (give to the poor). But if he himself is a poor man, it seems sufficient that he give whatever he can to charity, and the remainder of what his meal would have cost should feed the members of his household, which shall also be counted as charity, since his own life and the lives of his household come first.
Pele Yoetz 380:14: Also among the conditions of the fast is that he not publicize his fast. It is already told in Sefer Chasidim of a woman who used to reveal her fast and was punished for her fast - except at a time when many are fasting, such as during the days of Shovavim or the Ten Days of Repentance, when there is no prohibition against publicizing. This is a great principle in all of Judaism, and especially in matters of piety: that one fulfill (Micah 6:8), "and walk humbly with your God." Not only should he not reveal it, but he should conceal his deeds greatly and wish that they not be revealed - unlike many of the common people who do not reveal their pious acts, yet whose heart desires that it be revealed through someone else, so that their deeds be praised in the gates, to the point that they seek occasions and pretexts so that it come to be revealed, and when they see it has been revealed they act as though they wish to deny the matter and conceal their deeds, making themselves humble with their mouths while their heart walks in darkness, rejoicing and saying in their heart, "Blessed is He who reveals hidden things" - these are the mark of hypocrites. But the perfect man conceals his deeds as much as he can, even from the members of his own household, as I have written above under the entry Satar - unless he sinned a public sin causing desecration of the Name, in which case he must publicize his repentance, as written in Sefer Chasidim (section 167). And it is already told of the holy Rabbi Mahari Kuli, that once he undertook a three-day fast, and on the third day toward evening he needed to go to a wealthy man's house, and the wealthy man honored him with a coffee drink, and he drank it so as not to reveal that he was fasting - whoever does such things, the Name certainly accounts it to him as though he fasted a complete fast, with nothing diminished from its value.
Pele Yoetz 380:15: It is fitting for a person that on the fast day he not spend the whole day in business, but rather minimize his dealings and engage in Torah, in ethical books and fear of the Name. And how good and pleasant it is to study the order of the sacrifices, to fulfill what is said (Hosea 14:3), "and let us render the bulls of our lips." And let him examine his deeds and make a lengthy confession, and make fences and self-restrictions to repent from the transgressions in his hand, and pour out speech and seek forgiveness with abundant tears and a broken and contrite heart. And it is good to pray regarding the fast both at its beginning and its end - at its beginning, that the blessed Name help him do it properly, and at its end, that He accept it with favor (and I too intend, with the help of Heaven, to compose something on this and have included it in my Book of Prayers). These are some of the ways one should conduct the day of afflicting one's soul, and such shall be the fast the blessed God shall choose, and it shall be accepted to atone for him.
Pele Yoetz 381:1: Teshuvah (Repentance) - The obligation of repentance is explained in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and tripled in the Writings. And all the sages of Israel in every generation, early and late, new and old, all proclaim regarding repentance, as is explained in the Talmud, Midrashim, and all books of ethics and fear of the Name. Whoever desires life should be diligent about them day by day and let their words enter his ears, to observe, do, and fulfill the ways of repentance. For indeed it is said that the great essential thing for entering the paths of repentance is Torah study - that he study necessary laws and ethical books and books of fear of the Name. And whoever draws near, draws near to the dwelling of the Name, to study houses to teach or hear teachings, is closer to the Name, and goes on drawing nearer day by day, growing and increasing in unity [with God], advancing further in repentance. And whoever is far from Torah is far from the blessed Name, going and diminishing day by day until he tramples on transgressions and they become treated as permitted to him - either because he does not know the Torah's laws, and forbids what is permitted and permits what is forbidden, or even if he knows the prohibition, he does not know its severity, in the manner the commentators explained the verse (Genesis 6:5), "and every impulse of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all the day" - "only" is a diminishing term: the evil inclination diminishes the transgression and makes it seem small in his eyes. Or because since he transgressed a transgression and repeated it, it becomes to him as though permitted, in such a way that "the way of a fool is upright in his own eyes," to the point that if they tell him to repent, he would say, "What wrong is found in me that I should repent,"
Pele Yoetz 381:2: and what is repentance, and how do we make repentance - and because of this the fool walks in darkness and goes from evil to evil, until he leaves the world, going along weeping to the pit of destruction, may the Merciful One save us.
Pele Yoetz 381:3: Not so one who is diligent to study or hear teachings - he who walks with the wise shall become wise (Proverbs 13:20), and knows what is forbidden and its severity, that even for a light transgression he is considered like one who denies a fundamental principle, for he rebels against the kingdom in the presence of the great, mighty King, awesome and fearsome, whose glory fills the whole earth, and who watches over every step of man, man's thoughts and his schemes - nothing is hidden from Him; and it is known that the Holy One, blessed be He, repays good reward to the righteous and evil and bitter punishment for every transgression, even the lightest of the light, and is exacting to the width of a hair and forgives nothing, and the punishment is exceedingly, exceedingly great, to the point that it is said that if a person were to suffer all the days of his life sufferings like the sufferings of Job, it would be nothing compared to what the sinning soul undergoes on the day of death, and the day of death is nothing compared to what one undergoes in the World to Come - harsh and bitter punishments of various kinds, to the point that the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom, although it is exceedingly harsh as explained in the Midrashim, and "pass through the Valley of Weeping, making it a place of springs," where they shed rivers and streams of tears - even so, this is nothing compared to other judgments and reincarnations and the sling-throw [kaf hakela] and the like. And correspondingly, for one who increases this good trait, the reward of commandments is exceedingly great, as we have written above under the entries Shemi'ah and Sechar.
Pele Yoetz 381:4: And when a Jewish man reads the holy books, he shall see with his own eyes that what would not be counted to him as a sin is [actually] a criminal offense, and he shall clothe himself in dread, and he shall repent and be healed. And likewise he shall know the commandments thoroughly, and how the order of service to the blessed God works, and the segulah of Torah, which is a spice against the evil inclination, to the point that it is said (Kiddushin 30b): if this repulsive one [the evil inclination] encounters you, drag him to the study house - if he is stone, he shall dissolve; if he is iron, he shall shatter - in such a way that great is Torah, for it takes a person out of the ways of death into the ways of life. And whoever studies halachot and ethics every day, or hears it as though he studies it, is assured that he is destined for the World to Come, for the light within it returns him to the good. And this is why our sages, of blessed memory, instituted for us in the Amidah prayer, "Return us, our Father, to Your Torah, and bring us back in complete repentance before You" - for it is impossible for repentance to endure without prior engagement in Torah study.
Pele Yoetz 381:5: And this is the law of the penitent: when his heart is aroused, a pure heart, to return in repentance, he should not turn at first to self-mortifications and fasts, but rather fast a little, from time to time, or with light afflictions in the manner we have written above under the entry Ta'anit, and pour out his soul before the Name that He help him and dig for him a tunnel beneath His throne of glory to bring him back in repentance. And at first he shall abandon his wicked way and inquire from books and from authors regarding the statutes of God and His teachings, and which is the straight way to conduct himself with good traits and upright conduct. And he shall conduct himself in the ways of Judaism and uprightness and be diligent to fulfill every good thing, even matters of piety. He shall be careful and guard against any hint of transgression whatsoever unto the dissolution of the soul, and not transgress, as it is written (Deuteronomy 6:5), "And you shall love the Lord," etc., "with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might." And if his money is dear to him, even so he shall love the Name with all his money and not transgress his Maker's will, even if he must lose all his money, for "a person is very much recognized by his purse" - is he steadfast in the service of the blessed Name, or does he weaken? And it is written (Song of Songs 1:3), "Therefore the maidens love you" - our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Avodah Zarah 35b) "unto death they love you." Thus shall he do and conduct himself for some time, until he strengthens himself and it is assured to him, with the help of the Almighty, that he shall not return again to folly. And then he shall go to a modest, pious sage who is expert in remedies of the soul, and reveal to him the pains of his soul that have passed over him from the day of his birth, the raging waters, concealing nothing from him, and ask before him that he heal him and rectify him with good counsel, and not turn from what the teacher tells him, right or left, just as the sick person does not turn from the doctor's instruction - and then the sage shall act according to his wisdom and guide him with his counsel. For it is true that it is explained in the books of the disciples of the Ari and other kabbalists - rectifications of repentance for every sin and every transgression, a number of fasts according to the sin, and there are severe sins that require sitting in the sun during the summer months among ants, and on ice, and rolling naked in snow during the rainy months, and lashes, and nettles, and the like. And those who expound severities said that the notarikon of "teshuvah" [repentance] is: ta'anit (fast), sak (sackcloth), efer (ash), bechi (weeping), hesped (eulogy) - and likewise it is written (Joel 2:12), "Return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning."
Pele Yoetz 381:6: But I say that in this orphaned generation, if it happens that a Jewish man comes to a sage to give him rectifications and teach him the ways of repentance, one must be concerned for the leniency granted to penitents, and books such as these that speak of rectifications of repentance, with a number of fasts and self-mortifications, are forbidden to be read before the masses of the people, for absent this, through our sins, not even one person from a whole city would go to a sage to learn the ways of repentance, since he thinks he has no sin at all; and even if he knows the bitterness of his own soul, that severe transgressions have passed over his head, he thinks that abandoning his wicked way suffices, and "one who separates from sin is as one newly born" - and therefore no one at all comes to inquire of God and seek rectifications of repentance. And how much more so if he hears that he must afflict his soul with fasts and harsh self-mortifications - he shall despair of mercy entirely, for he shall say, "If I were to fast all my years, I would not manage to atone for my abundant transgressions, even if my strength were the strength of stones" - and because of this he may say there is no hope for him, and what is lost is lost, and he shall go and do whatever his heart desires. And how much more so since, in truth, not all times and not all people are equal, and it has already been said in the name of the Ari, of blessed memory, that the little done in these generations is considered as much as what was done in earlier generations, since the husk [kelipah] has grown strong and our strength has failed through our sins. And they said in the Talmud (Chullin 84a): Abba was from a family of healthy people, but such as we are, like Levites who merely eat [i.e., weaker stock] - what shall we, such as we are, answer? We are comparable to one who owes a great debt and is broken, and his hand cannot reach to pay in full - he speaks supplications like a poor man and shows his accounting until his creditor agrees to be repaid over time, in halves, in thirds, and in quarters, as his means allow - so are we all, broken, and we cannot fulfill our obligations; rather, let us do, little by little, what is in our power to do, to rectify our distortion during the days of our lives - perhaps God shall be entreated for us and forgive all our debts, but on condition that we do and accept all that is in our power to do.
Pele Yoetz 381:7: And if it should happen that an Israelite man comes to the sage to inquire of God and seek rectification for his sins and transgressions, he should not be strict with him at first; rather, he should tell him only, "Guard yourself and guard your soul greatly from every evil thing, and observe and fulfill every good thing." And when he strengthens himself and becomes habituated to this for a short time, he shall begin to tell him that he must rectify his distortion - and this is the first thing that emerges, a hard service and a strong trial: for if he can withstand it, he is assured that he shall fulfill all the ways of repentance. And this is what they said (Yoma 85b), that regarding transgressions between man and man there is no remedy at all until he appeases his fellow, and one who has robbery in his hand, his prayer is not heard (Shemot Rabbah 22:3), and one whose prayer is not heard, even on the Days of Awe, what remedy does he have at all? And greater than this, one might say that it is as though he has transgressions between man and man in his hand, and Yom Kippur does not atone for him even for transgressions between him and the Omnipresent.
Pele Yoetz 381:8: And the sin of robbery is exceedingly severe, for one who robs his fellow even of the value of a penny is as though he took his life and the blood of his offspring, as stated in the Shulchan Aruch (Choshen Mishpat, section 359, para. 3). Behold, therefore, whoever's spirit is moved with a steadfast spirit to return to his Creator must do this first: return the stolen item he stole and the extorted item he extorted, and appease his fellow, and whomever he provoked with words he shall appease until his fellow accepts him, and afterward he shall return to his Creator and be accepted.
Pele Yoetz 381:9: And it is true that this is an exceedingly hard thing from several aspects: one, from the aspect of shame, for like the shame of a thief when he is found breaking in, so shall he be ashamed to return the stolen item or ask forgiveness; and further, it is hard to return theft that has been consumed, and it may happen that if he comes to return thefts and damages from interest he consumed and the like, even his own belt is not his own. And there are those whose means cannot reach to pay the theft he stole and the extortion he extorted and the interest he consumed and the like, even if he were to sell himself and the members of his household. And there are those who robbed the public, such as through deficient weights, or robbed people he does not know and cannot repay, and there are many such obstacles that the evil inclination makes like a high wall and like a wall of iron, to the point that a person thinks it is impossible to repent. But the man whose spirit is moved to return to his Creator with all his heart and all his soul and all his might, as is fitting, shall not turn back for anyone's sake, and according to the pain is the reward. For it is said (Berachot 12b): whoever transgresses a transgression and is ashamed, all his sins are forgiven. And let a person believe with complete faith that whatever shame he suffers in this world is not one part in a thousand thousand of the shame and humiliation, confusion and disgrace, he shall suffer in the World to Come before the heavenly court, the myriads upon myriads of holy camps - woe to that shame, woe to that disgrace. And it is better for a person to be disgraced in this world and be forgiven, than to be disgraced in the World to Come and suffer harsh punishments. And if he cannot gather the strength to return the stolen item because his means are insufficient, there is a remedy through asking forgiveness; but if he has the means, he must surely return it, and what he returns shall be counted as great spirit, for "he who makes riches, but not by right, in the midst of his days shall leave them" (Jeremiah 17:11), "and his end shall be a fool," and forbidden money mixed with permitted money - this one comes and destroys that one; but by returning the stolen item, "the blessing of the Lord makes rich" (Proverbs 10:22).
Pele Yoetz 381:10: And if it is a robbery or theft of which the owners are unaware and were not distressed over it, he may return it without the owner's knowledge, by folding it into an accounting or the like, and he does not even need to appease him; but if he distressed his fellow and sinned against him, whether through his body, his money, or his honor, he is not forgiven until he appeases him - even if the injured party forgives him of his own accord and forgoes his own honor. And by the custom of the world where people say every night, "I hereby forgive and pardon," etc., this alone does not suffice, for while it helps a great deal, nevertheless the obligation rests upon the person himself to do what is incumbent upon him and to appease his fellow. Know this, for it is brought in the Talmud (Yoma 87a) of a servant of Rav, who used to go and humble himself before a certain butcher every eve of Yom Kippur so as to ask forgiveness for a maneh (a sum of money), so that it would serve as atonement for him - learn from this that it does not suffice for the injured party to forgive on his own alone, all the more so since a person does not even know whether his fellow has truly forgiven him, for among the many who recite the formula "I hereby forgive and pardon," their mouths and their hearts are not equal, and some do not even know what they are saying - and the proof is that on the following day, the grievance stands in its place with even greater force. Behold, then, it does not suffice without asking forgiveness; and if it is hard in his eyes to be shamed before his fellow face to face, he may do so through a messenger or through a letter, for indeed writing is a good remedy for anything hard to say out of shame - let his hand be written and his face not be seen by the one he wrongs. And Israel are holy and they are merciful, and surely when his Israelite brother comes to ask forgiveness of him, the one forgiving will not be cruel, and will immediately consent to grant him complete forgiveness, so that his Israelite brother not be punished on his account. And if he returns a stolen item, the victim should not accept it back as a gift, in accordance with the teaching of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Bava Kamma 94b): robbers and lenders on interest who make restitution - one does not accept it from them, and one who accepts from them, the sages are not pleased with him.
Pele Yoetz 381:11: And if he robbed the public, or does not know whom he robbed or whose money he consumed, there is a remedy through performing works for the public good. And there are public works that can be done with any small effort, such as, in a place where there is mud on the road, laying down a plank of wood or a stone and the like - there are many such things where the expense is small and the benefit great, and one should pursue them, for one who does these things rectifies what he distorted through robbery and fraud that he cannot otherwise repay, and it shall also be counted as a great mitzvah, for he is one who performs great kindness. And if he cannot do anything of public benefit, or if he robbed gentiles and his means cannot reach to make restitution, or if he is obligated to return the stolen item to young orphans who are not capable of forgiving, in a manner that he has no remedy, even so let him not despair of mercy, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures; rather let him pour out his soul before the Name that He help him for the sake of His own honor, and let him accept upon himself that when his means allow, he will make restitution, and the Lord shall look to the heart and have mercy on him, His maker.
Pele Yoetz 381:12: And regarding transgressions between man and the Omnipresent, let him afflict himself little by little as much as he can bear, and let him begin with a small amount and go on increasing, doing all that is in his power to do - fasts, self-mortifications and abstentions, sackcloth and lashes and nettles and the like. All that he adds to do, he adds to purify his soul and to purify what he has blemished, like soiled garments, for which a small washing helps somewhat, but the more one adds to launder them with lye and soap, the more they are purified and whitened. And even if he thinks he has already rectified his distortion, he should not refrain from afflicting his soul to purify the stains of the sins of Israel, for such is the judgment of one who loves the Name with a true love, who is not concerned for himself but only for the honor of his Maker, to the point that if it were possible for him to be told that through his self-affliction, if he wishes his own sins to be atoned, only one sin of his own will be atoned, but if he agrees that his affliction atone for his fellow's sins, two sins will be atoned - he would choose that his fellow's sins be atoned, so that there be more purity and more satisfaction above. Behold, then, it is good for a man to pray for the community of Israel as a whole, in order to ease the distress of the Shechinah and the distress of the Messiah and the distress of all the worlds, for this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 381:13: And all the more so, since in these generations we have grown exceedingly poor and lacking in all good, and there is no righteous man on earth whose heart would allow him to say that he has rectified his distortion and fully discharged his obligation, even if he were to live a thousand years, for there is not a moment without some mishap, and every day he adds new matters upon old ones, and there is none among us who knows how to direct the proper intentions and unifications to rectify our distortion as required through sackcloth and fasting; and even so, it was not accepted completely until Moses came and prayed (Deuteronomy 33:6), "Let Reuben live and not die." And so King David, peace be upon him, undertook the path of repentance, and afflicted himself so greatly that he said (Psalms 109:24), "My knees are weak from fasting," and how much suffering he bore, as explained in the words of our sages, of blessed memory, and even so it was not fully accepted until seven years after his passing, when the Temple was built. And we find that many great men of the world had their faces darkened from fasting over a light sin (Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat 25:5, Chagigah 22b). And for us, who are full of iniquities, surely all the days of our years would not suffice, and we cannot discharge our obligation.
Pele Yoetz 381:14: And we already have several clear signs to know that we have not yet been purified, for if our souls were purified, no mishap would come from our hands, nor anything improper, and we would be able to direct our minds to fear and love the Name with great fear and intense love, and to have proper intention in prayers, blessings and commandments, and foreign thoughts and evil musings would not confuse us against our will and to our own detriment, and we would be able to serve our Creator with complete service, perfect service, with fear and love and great joy as is proper, and we would grieve and be sorrowful in a time of sorrow, such as over the destruction of the Temple and over our sins and the pain we caused by them, like one whose only son has died and lies before him, and our soul would ascend on high every night to gaze upon the pleasantness of the Lord, and such and such is doubled and redoubled good for the righteous. Not so now, when our souls are not purified, we lack all good. And it was already written in Sefer HaCharedim, explaining the verse (Proverbs 27:21), "The refining pot is for silver and the furnace for gold, and a man is tested by his praise" - that just as gold is tested in the furnace to see if it is pure gold or full of dross, so a man is tested by his praise: if he can direct his heart in prayer to serve his Creator with complete service, perfect service, with fear and love and great joy, it shows that his soul is purified, and the opposite shows the opposite.
Pele Yoetz 381:15: And the man who is pure, the spirit of God will guide him with good counsel, and awaken him with great awakening to fulfill every commandment properly, each thing in its time. Not so we, whose sins withhold the good from us, and whose iniquities have separated between us and our Father in Heaven. And if a person should say he wishes to fulfill the rectifications of repentance as written in Sefer HaRokeach and the words of the Ari, of blessed memory, and the other books of the kabbalists, and to discharge his obligation - it is an impossible thing, for we who are full of iniquities, upon seeing their words, our bones would seize with trembling and our thoughts would terrify us at seeing the multitude of fasts required, and we would despair of mercy; all the more so, since who can count the number of sins he has committed all the days of his life, in this incarnation and in other incarnations. Therefore it is good for a man to afflict himself without counting, and all the days of his life to stand on guard, and to do all that is in his power to do; perhaps there is hope that we shall be reconciled to our Creator, who knows the greatness of our lowliness and our poverty and the smallness of our worth and the shortness of our understanding, and He deals charitably with us, and grants us from the treasury of the free gift. And indeed it is said (Berachot 9a), "Happy is the man who is always fearful" - this is written regarding words of Torah, and especially regarding the matter of repentance, one must never be complacent nor trust in himself, but must always fear lest he has not done what was required of him, and that beyond what he has rectified he has again spoiled matters through the transgressions he commits in their ordinary course, or perhaps he has rectified nothing at all, and his repentance was not accepted, such as if he became angry - for one who becomes angry tears his own soul in his anger. And our teacher the Ari wrote that for one who becomes angry, all the commandments and good deeds he has accumulated for himself all go over to the Sitra Achra together with his soul, which goes to the Sitra Achra, and he has no remedy at all forever, until he accepts upon himself not to become angry, and only then can he begin to make rectification. And likewise if he did his repentance in order to be seen and to be praised, it is an abomination to the Lord. And there are likewise several transgressions that cause the gates of repentance to be locked before him, particularly the sin of wasteful emission of seed, of which it is said in the holy Zohar that he has no repentance except through exceedingly great effort in repentance.
Pele Yoetz 381:16: And even so, let him not despair of mercy, and let him not say, "I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and futility," but rather let him trust in the Name that it is possible he has rectified what he had distorted and found the means of his redemption, and let him believe with complete faith that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of any good thing whatsoever, and does not despise or loathe any affliction of the afflicted, and has not hidden His face from him, but rather it is that none of us knows what man is, and what will become of his judgment until the day of death - only then will man know his worth, when he finds himself in the land of the living. To what may this be compared? To a king's son whom his father sent from the place called Truth to a distant land, so that he might profit and make a good name for himself; but he did not do so, but rather turned to reckless companions and borrowed and ate and was satisfied and grew fat, and the debt rose to a great sum, and he did not know the total, and the creditors went to the king to demand payment, and the king told them to wait until it be written to his son that he see to mend his ways, and to strive with all his might to earn and send enough to fully repay what he had borrowed, for if he did not do so, the king would bring him before him and exact payment from his body and soul. And so the king's son did, and he began to send money and goods to his father so that his debts be paid; but he is afraid day and night lest he has not yet sent even a third or a fourth, or even two percent of what he owes, for he does not know the total of the debt, and lest robbers stole on the way what he sent, or lest his goods were not accepted in the place called Truth and went to waste, for there nothing passes except what is pure, clean, and select. And so he keeps sending more and more, and forever lives in this fear, until he himself goes to the place called Truth and sees what he has done and made - if his work is pure and upright, then his heart shall rejoice and his glory shall exult, for there he shall find a lasting principal. And the parable is understood of itself - examine it and you will find it so. And who is greater to us than Rabbi Abbahu, to whom thirteen rivers of pure balsam oil were shown [in a dream as his reward in the World to Come], and yet he said, "I have labored in vain" (Bereishit Rabbah 62:2, cf. Ta'anit 25a). And this is the fear of sin that leads to holiness, and of this it is said (Psalms 34:10), "Fear the Lord, His holy ones."
Pele Yoetz 381:17: Behold, then, happy is the man who fears the transgressions in his hand, and let him do ever more, and let it seem in his own eyes as though he has done nothing at all. Who is greater to us than King David, peace be upon him, who, after having done wondrous deeds, nevertheless said (Psalms 51:5), "And my sin is ever before me" - how much more so we, orphans of orphans, who do not even know what we are, what we have sinned, and what we have come to rectify; surely all our sins and iniquities must forever be arranged before our eyes. And there is great value in this, for even if a person rises in status and is honored among people, and his inclination entices him to grow haughty, when he remembers his iniquities and transgressions and the sins of his youth, his heart will be humbled and he will lower himself and regard himself as base and despised in his own eyes, for he will say, "What is it to me to boast of imagined honor, that people whose eyes are but flesh honor me - do I not know my own transgression? And if my neighbors could smell it upon them, they would keep their distance from me and from my borders." And also, when he remembers his sins and keeps them before his eyes, he will not become angry at those under his authority if they do not carry out his will as he wishes, and he will not insist upon his own honor, and he will come to acquire the trait of humility.
Pele Yoetz 381:18: And since it is not in our power to rectify our distortion through fasts and self-mortifications in the measure appropriate to the essence of our sins, nor through intentions in unifications and pairings of the supernal attributes and such things as the perfect men who know how to fence in breaches do, upon whom then have we to rely but our Father in Heaven, who is appeased through mercy and won over through supplications and hears the prayer of every mouth. Behold, then, it is among the essentials of repentance that the poor man speak supplications, pour out his conversation, seek forgiveness from the Lord of lords, at the beginning of the night watches which is a time of favor - let him not fail to do this every night, especially on the long winter nights; let his heart pour out like water and his tears fall with a lowered voice of supplication, in bitterness of soul and great humility, as he takes to heart the greatness of his lowliness and poverty and the essence of his sins, and how bad and bitter it is to forsake the Name; let his heart writhe within him, let him find distress and grief and sigh in bitterness that breaks his whole body - for it has already been written that among the essentials of repentance are the grief and sorrow that one feels over his sins, and according to the greatness of the grief and sorrow, so he increases his purification, and this is a sign of purity.
Pele Yoetz 381:19: And there are already many openings and grounds for hatred and it is fitting that the sinning soul grieve and be embittered with weeping and bitter lamentation. And the more he grieves and weeps upon seeing that his soul is not purified and that the radiance of the Shechinah has grown distant from him - the proof of this is that he cannot grieve in his soul as much as would be proper, and his eyes do not shed streams of water on their own without forced effort, more than one would for a person whose dead lies before him as would be proper - such and such things should he take to heart, things that embitter the heart, so that his heart be humbled, and let the poor man speak supplications like a poor man begging at the door, for humility is a great gate for the acceptance of prayers (and I myself composed a prayer text with the help of Heaven and included it in my Book of Prayers, with the help of the blessed Name). And he may recite the texts of confessions and prayers of Yom Kippur, all of whose words are like coals of fire. And there are already in the books also texts of prayers for pouring out one's speech, for seeking forgiveness, such as in the book Shevet Musar and the book Shnei Luchot HaBrit and the book Tikun HaNefesh and the book Sha'arei Tzion and the like - how good it would be to recite them all, one each day, for the merit of their authors will stand by him so that his prayer be accepted. And one who does not understand the holy tongue should go to a sage to arrange for him a prayer in the vernacular, so that he may pray from the depths of his heart, and he should persist in prayer every single day of his life; perhaps he will find a time of favor when his prayer will be accepted.
Pele Yoetz 381:20: And let him always be truly humble, base and despised in his own eyes, one of those who are insulted but do not insult, even toward the members of his own household, and let him forgo his own honor, and not insist at all on the honor due from those under his authority, remembering that he himself has angered his Creator, and through this the Lord will be reconciled to him and will atone for the sin he committed against his own soul. And likewise regarding all the things that serve as segulot for atonement, as we have written above under the entry Segulah, the penitent should pursue them to bring satisfaction to his Maker and be reconciled and atoned - and all in proportion to the greatness of his love, everything will seem easy in his eyes, and he will do more than is in his power to do; the weak one should say, "I am mighty," in order to merit rectifying his distortion and bringing satisfaction to his Maker, and to gaze upon the pleasantness of the Lord and visit in His sanctuary.
Pele Yoetz 381:21: And behold, although repentance is desirable at all times, as it is written (Psalms 90:3), "You return man to dust, saying, Return, O children of man," even to the crushing of the soul (Jerusalem Talmud, Chagigah 2:1), the essence of repentance is in the days of youth, as King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 12:1), "And remember your Creator in the days of your youth." And so our sages, of blessed memory, explained the verse (Psalms 112:1), "Happy is the man who fears the Lord" - meaning, happy is the one who repents while he is still a man (Avodah Zarah 19a), that is, a young man - not like the many fools among the people who say, "Youth comes but once," and the evil inclination says (Ecclesiastes 11:9), "Rejoice, young man, in your youth." And there are precious young men whom the fear of the Name has touched in their hearts, who wish to hear the words of the wise and walk in the ways of the good, but they are ashamed before their wicked companions who mock them with words of scorn and derision and laughter, calling him a "foolish pietist," until they are kept from doing good - woe to the mockers, alas for them! And the sages of ethics have already written that they are like a highway robber who stands on the road and robs those bringing an offering to the king, for surely the king will pursue him and put him to a cruel death with harsh and bitter punishments; and this is the evil of man on earth, that when he walks in the way of sinners, he wants and desires that others be like him, so that the distress of the many be the comfort of fools, but this is not the way for one whose heart has been touched by love of the Name, as we wrote a parable on this above under the entry Ahavat Re'im. But the man who desires life should strive greatly to act in secret and walk modestly; yet if he cannot, he should not refrain from doing good for fear of the mockery of the complacent, and should not turn back for anyone's sake, for it is better for a person to be called a fool all his days than to be wicked before the Omnipresent for even one hour. And just as in a place of monetary profit one is not concerned about mockery and scorn, and says, "I will sit there and let people laugh," all the more so should one not be deterred from bringing satisfaction to his Maker, who pays a good reward to those who walk in purity.
Pele Yoetz 381:22: And the obligation to give priority to repentance in the days of youth is for several reasons. This is the first: a person cannot be assured of the days of his life, that he will reach old age, and especially in these generations death is common, and it is found more often that young men die, may the Merciful One save us, than that old men die. And how precious are the words of the Tanna Rabbi Eliezer who said (Avot 2:10), "Repent one day before your death" - repent today, lest you die tomorrow, and thus all your days will be spent in repentance. Furthermore, if a person says, "I will rejoice in my youth, and when the days of old age come I will repent," this is like one who says, "I will sin and then repent," of whom it is said that he is not given the means to make repentance (Yoma 88a, cf. 85b). Furthermore, God will bring everything into judgment, and the days of youth do not exempt him from his turn - on the contrary, the days of youth, when his strength is in him and he is a man of vigor, are the fitting time to expend his energy on the Torah and to run like a deer and be mighty as a lion in the service of his Creator and to fulfill the ways of repentance. And according to the many years and the many good deeds and repentance he performs, so he increases the purification and rectification of his distortion, and perhaps he will find the means of his redemption; for although repentance is desirable even on the day of death, that is only so that he not be punished for having transgressed the word of the Merciful One, for which confession and remorse alone suffice - but to purify his soul and rectify what he has distorted, and to silence the accusers created by his sins, he will suffer harsh and bitter punishments until he is purified, as we wrote above under the entry Ta'anit. Furthermore, repentance in the days of youth, while his strength is still in him and his blood is still hot within him, is desirable and is accepted to a much greater degree and increases purification, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 86b), "Who is a true penitent? One who, at the same period, in the same place, with the same woman," etc., refrains - in such a way that shows that his repentance is out of love and fear of his Maker and not because of weakened strength and the cessation of his desire. Furthermore, when a person repents in the days of his childhood and youth, the burden of sins will not weigh so heavily upon him, and perhaps he will manage to be purified within many years; not so if he does not repent until old age and gray hair, for then his sin is too great to bear, weighing upon him like a heavy burden, and given the fewness of his remaining years and the weakening of his strength, he will not be able to be fully purified, but will be left to suffer punishments in the World to Come. Furthermore, when a person accustoms himself to an evil way and treads in it until it becomes to him as though permitted, even when he grows old he will not turn from it. And there are yet other reasons for which there is no need to elaborate, and childhood and youthful vigor are vanity - happy is the man who fears the Name and remembers his Creator in the days of his youth, and turns from his evil way and walks in the way of the good, and keeps to the paths of the righteous (Proverbs 2:20).
Pele Yoetz 381:23: In any case, if the days of youth have passed and one comes on in years, the obligation of repentance grows greater upon him when he sees gray hair sprinkled upon him, for he is already close to death with one foot in the grave, and if not now, when? And if he does not repent then, his punishment will grow doubly greater for not having had pity on his own soul and on the honor of his Maker when the day of his calamity draws near - he thereby becomes liable for his own life. Therefore, while his eyes are still open, before the days of evil come, let him hasten and make haste to find refuge for himself, to fulfill the ways of repentance as much as he can bear, and let him do all that is in his power to do, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures, and perhaps he will be able to purify his soul; and in any case, whatever atonement he achieves is an atonement achieved and a rescue accomplished. And let a person not despair of mercy, saying, "My iniquities have passed over my head, they weigh upon me like a heavy burden, and there is no recovery for my downfall, and since I am lost, I am lost, therefore I shall do whatever my heart desires and see good in this world" - this is the counsel of the evil inclination, or it is that his sins withhold the good from him and lock the doors of repentance before him. Therefore they do to him one of two things: either he does not feel his sickness and his evil, for his own eyes have flattered him into thinking that his way is upright in his own eyes, or he despairs of mercy and does whatever his heart desires.
Pele Yoetz 381:24: And the Tanna already warned against this and said (Avot 2:13), "Do not be wicked in your own eyes," and our sages, of blessed memory, warned (Kiddushin 40b) that a person should always regard himself as though he were half meritorious and half guilty, and regard the whole world as though it were half meritorious and half guilty: if he performs one commandment, happy is he, for he has tipped the scale for himself and for the whole world toward merit; if he commits one transgression, woe to him, for he has tipped the scale for himself and for the whole world toward guilt - for the scale and balance of judgment are in the hand of the God of knowledge, the Lord; there is a commandment that outweighs several transgressions, and there is a transgression that outweighs several commandments, according to what kind of person he is and according to the matter. Behold, then, let a man gather strength so that he might have one less transgression and fulfill one more commandment; and even if it were as he says, that his sins are many, still, every additional transgression he commits increases his punishment, for the judgment of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not like the judgment of flesh and blood, which cannot put the guilty to death more than once, whether for one transgression or for many transgressions, and therefore since he is already condemned to death he might as well do whatever his heart desires and curse the king - but the Holy One, blessed be He, is not so; rather He gives to the wicked according to his wickedness, and if he performs even one commandment, even if he is otherwise wholly guilty, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold his reward, but he merits great good for that one commandment. And if he does a little of the ways of repentance, it will be deducted from his punishment, and everything is added to the account like a shopkeeper who extends credit, who collects even in small coins, and every small coin is added to the reckoning; and to one who is like the dead, who does not feel the scalpel, so he does not feel his own sickness and evil and the distress of his soul. "The way of life is the rebukes of discipline" - let him strengthen himself to teach books of ethics or to hear them taught, perhaps there is hope that he will awaken from his sleep. And let him also pour out his soul before the Name that He dig for him a tunnel beneath His throne of glory to bring him back in repentance.
Pele Yoetz 381:25: And our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, already composed a text to be said within the blessing of Hashivenu during the Ten Days of Repentance, brought in the books on the Days of Awe in the prayer for the Fast of Gedaliah, and I, the poor one, added to it some words, and thus one should say it always, every day:
Pele Yoetz 381:26: "Bring us back, our Father, to Your Torah, and draw us near from our heart to Your service, and return us in complete repentance before You. Please, God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger - be patient until we return to You in complete repentance before You, and until we complete the rectification of our soul, our spirit, and our neshamah; and dig a tunnel beneath Your throne of glory to return us in complete repentance before You and to guide us to Your service, and be reconciled to us in Your abundant mercies, for Your right hand is outstretched to receive the penitent. Blessed are You, Lord, who desires repentance."
Pele Yoetz 381:27: Let every person pray over this and beg for great mercy, for this is a grievous sickness, and this is called a distress more bitter than death, for since he does not feel his sickness and does not seek a remedy for his wound, who will heal him? Behold, he perishes and is lost, God forbid. Therefore, while he is still alive, let him cry out before the Name every day like the groaning of a slain man, for He revives the dead with great mercy.
Pele Yoetz 381:28: And behold, the time for repentance is all the days of a person's life, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year, as our teaching of Rabbi Eliezer states (Avot 2:10), "Repent one day before your death." And it is already said in the holy Zohar that it is fitting for a person that every night before he goes to sleep he examine his deeds of that day, and if he finds that he has committed a transgression or done something not good, let him confess and feel remorse and rectify his distortion as best he can, through some form of self-mortification or some fine for charity and the like; and such people the holy Zohar calls "the wary ones, masters of accounting." And it is explained in the holy Zohar that the Torah warned about this (Deuteronomy 21:23), "You shall not let his corpse remain overnight," meaning that one should not spend the night together with his sin, for it is a carcass. And the commentators wrote that one who repents immediately, on the same day, can more easily rectify his distortion, for it resembles wet ink which can easily be erased and wiped clean, unlike when it has dried. And if he did not repent on that day, let him at least repent on the sixth day of that week, which is also a time for repentance.
Pele Yoetz 381:29: And it is fitting for a person to bring forward thoughts of repentance so that he may be called "holy," which is a form of testimony, and the wicked is disqualified from testimony; and also so that he merit an added measure of nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, and the illumination of having sanctified the Sabbath, and from the radiance and abundance of its holiness he will draw influence upon himself for the weekdays to return in repentance and to serve his Creator with complete service. Therefore it is good for a man to set aside his affairs before accepting the Sabbath and pour out his speech, seek forgiveness, and afterward go to the immersion house, and he will find benefit for his soul, and it will purify him and sanctify him.
Pele Yoetz 381:30: And also the eve of the New Moon is a time for repentance, for what he sinned in that past month. And already many men of good deeds are accustomed to fast every eve of the New Moon and to increase supplications, and the day is called in the books "the small Day of Atonement." And we have already written that the fast itself is not the main point, but rather the repentance - that he turn from his evil way and confess and forsake it; then He will have mercy.
Pele Yoetz 381:31: And if all year he walked in the stubbornness of his heart and his inclination cast a deep sleep upon him, then when the days of desire, the days of favor arrive - the month of mercy and the Ten Days of Repentance - it is not a time to slumber and sleep, for "a king by justice establishes the land" (Proverbs 29:4), and he should clothe himself in dread and awaken like a man roused from his sleep. Happy are Israel - most of them arise to say Selichot at the first watches of the night, and the people increase somewhat their study of the book of Tikunim and the twenty-four books, Mishnayot and Psalms, each according to his own capacity, and there are few indeed who are not awakened in these days - the Torah does not speak of the dead. But it is a simple matter that it is not enough merely to recite Selichot and study a little to restrain transgression and put an end to the sins of the whole year and of all one's days; and if after Yom Kippur he returns to his former ways, what has he accomplished and what has he done - and He who sits in heaven will laugh at him and say, "Is it because Yom Kippur has passed that there is no fear of God before your eyes? Did you think you could hide and flee? Is the hand of the Lord too short to punish such a man all year, who mocks Me as one mocks a fellow man, saying to Him, 'I will do as You say' until he escapes from His hand - can you flee from before Me?" Rather, these days are remembered and become, for the man who fears and is tender of heart regarding the transgressions in his hand, an occasion that he should set aside his affairs a little each day, and take in hand the great order of confession found in the books, and fix his eye upon it, item by item, to take an accounting, and reckon with his Maker all that he has not done well from the things written in the confession, from the day he came into being upon the earth until that very day. And if there is something in which he still persists in its impurity, let him feel complete remorse, and accept upon himself with all his strength never to return to folly again. And if it is something difficult for him to separate from entirely, let him fence himself in with restrictions and safeguards and penalties and the like, to stand guard and to be careful of any trace of sin whatsoever, and to fulfill every matter and not transgress. And for that which he did not do well, and which caused great blemish and great damage and corrupted his soul and defiled and sullied it, let him do this: let him accept upon himself to afflict his soul that year with self-mortifications, fasts, and afflictions as much as he can bear, little by little, and let him record all these things in a true writing, what he has accepted to do. And it is best that he not accept upon himself more than a month or a single week at a time, and every week he should review what he has written, to see whether he has stood guard, and if he has breached it, let him fence the breach and continue to add on. And after doing all these things, on each of these mighty days he should confess with a bitter soul, and pour out his speech, seek forgiveness, for these are days of favor and his prayer and his repentance bear fruit.
Pele Yoetz 381:32: And it is written in the books that there is a difference between the Ten Days of Repentance and the rest of the days regarding repentance and prayer, like the difference between light and darkness, and one hour of repentance and good deeds in these days is worth more than whole days in the rest of the year; therefore one should be careful about every moment of these days so as not to waste it. And one whose Torah is his profession should, in these days, set aside his occupation with dialectics and be engaged only in reading books of ethics and in the ways of repentance, and in pouring out his speech, seeking forgiveness, and offering prayer in advance against every trouble that it not come. Happy is he who can seclude himself to reckon with his Maker, clothed in holy linen. And at the very least, in these days let him bring the two daily offerings as their law requires: "I have set the Lord before me always," and "my sin is ever before me." And if he finds a good companion, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together also - two are better than one, then those who fear the Lord speak with one another (Malachi 3:16) about which is the straight way, and each helps his fellow, and says to his brother, "Be strong."
Pele Yoetz 381:33: And well known is the teaching of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Kiddushin 30b), "A person's inclination overpowers him every day and seeks to kill him." And they said (Berachot 29a), "Do not trust in yourself until the day of your death," for Yochanan the High Priest served in the High Priesthood for eighty years and in the end became a Sadducee. Behold, then, one must stand on guard, and this is the way for one who wishes to enter into the paths of repentance and piety - this is the gate of the Lord: let him accept upon himself with all firmness never to fail to be diligent, day after day, to study a portion of the books of ethics, one page or one chapter, or to hear it taught, on condition of keeping, doing, and fulfilling it. These are some of the paths for one who wishes to return to the Lord, that He may have mercy on him, and to our God, for He will abundantly pardon.
Pele Yoetz 382:1: Tochachah (Rebuke) - Rebuke is one of the six hundred and thirteen positive commandments, as it is written (Leviticus 19:17), "You shall surely rebuke your fellow and not bear sin because of him." And this commandment is incumbent upon all of Israel, not as many of the common people suppose, that this commandment was given only to the sage of the city - this is not so; rather, every Jew is obligated to rebuke his fellow when he sees him transgressing a sin or refraining from fulfilling a commandment. And the obligation is even greater for the ordinary people, for their words bear more fruit than the words of the sage, since if the sage rebukes him, they will say, "He is a sage, he is a pious man, who can act as he does; if we were all like him, the Messiah would have come" - as if the coming of the Messiah were something impossible for us to bring about. Furthermore, the sage is not regularly found among the common people and does not see their deeds, unlike his fellow who is accustomed to being near him; and when he rebukes them and says to them, "Please, my brothers, do not do evil, and I too have a heart like yours to do as you do, but I am fearful of sin, for God will bring everything into judgment, and why should we not have regard for the honor of our Creator and become among those of whom it is said (Proverbs 17:25), 'A foolish son is a vexation to his father and bitterness to her who bore him' - and why should we not have regard for our own souls and destroy ourselves knowingly?" - such and such things one man speaks to his fellow, and his words bear fruit.
Pele Yoetz 382:2: And it is known that all Israel are sureties for one another, as it is written (Leviticus 26:37), "And they shall stumble, one man over his brother" - meaning, one man because of the sin of his brother, and "when one is taken to task, all are punished with him" (Bava Kamma 92a). And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 54b) that whoever sees his fellow committing a transgression and does not rebuke him to his face, Scripture regards it as though he himself had committed it, and he is punished first, as we find (ibid.) regarding the destruction of the Temple, as it is written (Ezekiel 9:6), "And begin at My sanctuary" - read it as "begin with My sanctified ones." And although the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "It is revealed and known before Me that they would not have accepted rebuke from them," the attribute of justice argued and said, "If it is revealed before You, was it revealed before them?" and death was decreed upon them even though they had kept the Torah from Aleph to Tav. And in Sefer Chasidim (section 153) it is written that whoever sees his fellow committing a transgression, and his fellow does not rebuke him, and he dies in it, it is considered as though he had killed him, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will demand his blood from his hand; and if he rebuked him and he did not heed his voice, what is written of him? (Ezekiel 3:19), "But you, because you warned the wicked... he shall die for his iniquity, but you have saved your soul." And they said (Sefer Chasidim, section 5) that one who rebukes his fellow and his fellow does not heed his voice takes his merits from him.
